pa_a_main_wall.blurb: The first wall most visitors meet at Birdsboro, a former quarry in Berks County, this is an upper-level face of machine-cut diabase with 27 bolted lines. Grades start around 5.6 and run to the low 5.12s, with the bulk between 5.8 and 5.11, so it suits both newer leaders and people working harder moves. Routes are short and the stone is blocky; expect some loose pieces, and polish on the easier lines because the wall sees steady traffic. Sun and shade are not well documented, so plan for either. The wall is reached from the main parking area by crossing the footbridge and bearing right at the trail split.

pa_n_beer_wall_reservoir_level.blurb: Beer Wall is a low-lying section of the old Birdsboro quarry, set down by the reservoir. It holds 23 bolted lines on short, mostly slabby faces of diabase, running from 5.7 up to about 5.11 with most falling between 5.7 and 5.9. That makes it a friendly place to warm up or to introduce someone to leading, and the low height suits practising cleaning and lowering. Like the rest of the quarry the walls were cut by machine, so check holds before trusting them. To get here, take the broad path downhill from the entrance toward the water and swing left around the fence.

pa_main_wall_3.blurb: The main face at Shaffer Rocks, a small crag beside the Appalachian Trail in Michaux State Forest near Caledonia, south-central Pennsylvania. The wall stands around 50 feet tall, a little higher toward its west end, and is made of solid Weverton quartzite. Almost everything here is set up for top-roping, with just a single trad line, and there are 26 routes from easy 5.3 terrain through the 5.8 to 5.11 range. Because the face looks north it stays shaded, yet the rock dries quickly. A good pick for a relaxed day with a group or newer climbers.
pa_main_wall_3.approach: A short walk on the blue-blazed trail brings you to the ledge below the face; the wall's base is under 100 yards from the old stone cabin.

pa_proving_grounds.blurb: A compact, tucked-away cluster of sandstone boulders in the hills above Ohiopyle, in southwestern Pennsylvania. The 25 problems range from VB through the V5 level, with a smaller run of seriously hard problems between V8 and V10, and the area is best known for tall, committing highball lines on very good stone. Boulders sit close together, so the main zone feels crowded with only a handful of people. It is a short walk from the road, but the way in is easy to miss, so bring a GPS track. Expect to bring several pads and a spotter.

pa_boulder_view.blurb: Part of Rocky Ridge County Park in York County, this spot has 24 problems on conglomerate outcrops tucked in the woods. Expect roofs, traverses and short crack lines on two main rock groups: one with a prominent ledge and overhanging roof, the other with gently overhanging sides. Problems are mostly easy to moderate, from VB to V4, so it is a relaxed spot for newer boulderers and families, and the ledge is a popular lookout for hikers too. It is a half-mile hike from the power lines, following the red blazes through the trees. Bring a pad or two.
